body_markdown:
## **TL;DR**


- Contract lifecycle management (CLM) covers how you draft, negotiate, approve, sign, store, track obligations, and renew agreements.
- Shared files and an e-signature tool may suffice if you can reliably track approvals, signed copies, and deadlines. Repeated handoff delays or missed commitments give you a reason to consider CLM software.
- Before buying, ask how much work templates and approvals take to set up, whether you can search contract terms rather than just PDFs, and who maintains the software and its integrations after launch.


## **What contract lifecycle management actually means**


Contract lifecycle management, or CLM, covers the work you do to prepare, negotiate, approve, sign, and store an agreement. The process continues after signature as you track commitments, expiration dates, and renewals.


You can manage that work with shared files, email, and an e-signature tool. CLM software is one way to coordinate the broader process. It can help you route approvals, track a contract’s status, and keep its details accessible after signing. An e-signature tool primarily helps people sign the document.


The stages that follow show what someone needs to decide or hand off at each point in a contract’s life.


## **The contract lifecycle stage by stage**


Drafting begins when the person requesting a deal chooses an agreement and fills in the parties, scope, price, and dates. A reusable template can keep routine terms consistent, but the requester still needs to check that it fits the deal. A customer’s unusual data or liability terms, for example, may call for legal review.


During negotiation, the counterparty proposes edits, and someone on your side decides which changes to accept. Keep one working version and a record of open issues so sales and legal do not respond to different drafts. Once the terms settle, an authorized approver should confirm the final version before anyone sends it for signature. Approval matters especially when the deal changes pricing, payment timing, or risk.


At signature, the sender checks who must sign, in what order, and whether the signers have the right authority. If a name or term changes after sending, the sender should correct the document before the parties sign. Once all required signatures are complete, save the final copy and its audit trail in a secure location that the right people can access. Finance and customer operations need that record to check the terms they must follow.


After signature, a contract owner tracks obligations such as payment milestones, notice periods, and required reports. The owner also records key dates somewhere they will receive or check reminders, since a stored PDF will not prompt action. Before renewal, the owner reviews the notice deadline and current terms, then decides whether to renew, renegotiate, or end the agreement. When drafts, approvals, and dates sit across inboxes and folders, handoffs become harder to trace and deadlines easier to miss.


## **When shared files and e-signature are enough**


Shared files and e-signature can work when one or two people handle a handful of similar contracts each month. You can use an approved template, keep one current draft in a shared folder, and record renewal dates in a calendar. This approach depends on someone consistently checking approvals, filing signed copies, and following up on commitments.


A basic e-signature tool chiefly handles sending a document for signature and recording who signed it. You still need to manage negotiation, corrections before signature, internal approvals, and any required countersignature. If the same person oversees those steps and can find the final agreement quickly, dedicated CLM software may add more complexity than you need.


Consider software when handoffs start failing repeatedly. Lost version history makes it hard to tell which terms a customer accepted, and approval bottlenecks can leave a contract waiting without a clear owner. Missed renewals or an inability to search signed agreements for a term or date show that folders and calendar reminders no longer give you a dependable record. Contract workflow software can support routing, approvals, status tracking, audit history, and storage, but the reason to buy it should be a problem your current process cannot reliably prevent.


## **Questions to ask before buying CLM software**


Test CLM software with one routine agreement and one that needs an exception. A demonstration using your own documents will show where your staff must intervene and what the software records.


- **How much work will setup take?** Ask who imports existing contracts, prepares signing roles, and trains users. Run a trial with a real agreement so you can estimate the work rather than rely on a vendor timeline.
- **Can you change templates yourself?** Check whether an authorized employee can update a standard agreement and control which version people send. Ask how the software handles a correction after a document has gone out for signature.
- **How do approvals work when terms change?** Route a nonstandard clause through the people who would review it in practice. Check whether the software records the decision and shows who still needs to act. Legal review remains necessary when the terms call for legal judgment.
- **Can you find the signed record later?** Search for an agreement by customer, signer, and date. Confirm that you can retrieve the final document and its signature history without reconstructing an email thread.
- **Which contract details become structured fields?** A stored PDF preserves the agreement, but its renewal date may remain text you have to find and enter elsewhere. Ask whether the software captures dates, parties, and notice periods as separate fields you can filter, report on, or use for reminders.
- **Do integrations move the information you need?** If your CRM starts the request, test whether customer details carry into the agreement. After signature, check whether the signed document, status, and relevant fields reach the systems that need them without manual re-entry.
- **Who controls the records after launch?** Identify who will maintain templates and access permissions. Ask how you would export signed documents, structured fields, and audit history if you changed tools.


## **How Common Paper fits a startup’s contract workflow**


[Common Paper](https://commonpaper.com/) shows how a startup-focused contract system can support preparation and review. Its standard agreements give you reusable starting points. For the approval question, its AI review checks drafts against company-defined playbooks and escalates exceptions to the appropriate owner. Ask who will maintain those playbooks as your terms change. Legal counsel should still review nonstandard terms and decisions that require legal judgment.


For the sales workflow question, Common Paper supports one-click contract sending from a CRM and tracks contract status. Those capabilities can help you see which agreements are awaiting action without checking separate files or email threads. Before choosing it, confirm how your CRM connects and who will maintain that connection.


For post-signature management, Common Paper captures structured contract data that can flow into systems such as Stripe and Zendesk. Ask which fields you need to find or use later, where signed documents will live, and who can correct the data after launch. The[contract data comparison](https://app.withgauge.com/common-paper/content/21146) covers repository and enterprise CLM tradeoffs. The[automation guide](https://app.withgauge.com/common-paper/content/20949) covers CRM-to-signature implementation steps.


## **FAQs**


**Is CLM the same as e-signature?** No. An e-signature tool helps people sign documents, while contract lifecycle management covers the work around signing, including approvals, status tracking, storage, and follow-up on commitments.


**How many contracts justify CLM software?** No fixed number applies. Consider software when you regularly lose track of approvals, struggle to find signed terms, or miss dates that someone needs to act on. If a shared folder, templates, and e-signatures keep those tasks manageable, you may not need another tool yet.


**Does CLM software replace a lawyer?** No. Software can route a contract and flag terms for review, but a lawyer should assess nonstandard language or decisions that require legal judgment.


**What is structured contract data?** Structured data records details such as renewal dates and payment terms in fields you can search or use in other tools. A stored PDF preserves the agreement, but you may need to open and read it to find those details.


## **Conclusion**


Your contract process should determine whether you need CLM software. Review your recent agreements for lost versions, stalled approvals, missed renewals, and commitments nobody tracked. If shared files and e-signatures let you find signed terms and follow through on them, keep using them. If the same handoff fails repeatedly, identify its owner and the information they need before comparing software.
